clinicalPearls: A rare benign condition characterised by multiple submucosal cartilaginous and bony nodules projecting into the lumen of the trachea and large bronchi
Characteristically spares the posterior membranous wall of the trachea because the nodules arise from cartilage, which is absent posteriorly
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally; when symptomatic it causes chronic cough, wheeze, haemoptysis, hoarseness, and recurrent infections
Bronchoscopy shows a distinctive cobblestone or rock-garden appearance with hard nodules that can make instrumentation difficult
CT demonstrates calcified nodules along the anterolateral tracheal walls with sparing of the posterior membrane
Usually a disease of older adults and generally follows a slow, benign course
Diagnosis is typically made bronchoscopically or on imaging, with biopsy confirming cartilage and bone within the nodules
reference.pathophysiology: Tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica is defined by the formation of multiple submucosal nodules composed of cartilage and heterotopic bone, sometimes with marrow, that bulge into the airway lumen. These nodules are thought to arise from the perichondrium and cartilaginous rings, which explains their anterolateral distribution and the characteristic sparing of the posterior membranous wall that lacks cartilage. The cause is unknown, with proposed contributions from chronic inflammation, metabolic and degenerative processes, and abnormal bone morphogenetic signalling within airway connective tissue. Over time the nodules can narrow and stiffen the airway, causing airflow obstruction, impaired secretion clearance, and recurrent infection.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis affecting the airway
additionalInvestigations: Bronchoscopy revealing the cobblestone nodular appearance and sparing of the posterior wall
CT of the airways showing calcified submucosal nodules
Biopsy demonstrating cartilage and bone within nodules
Pulmonary function tests including flow-volume loops for fixed obstruction
Assessment for recurrent infection and secretion retention
Exclusion of amyloidosis and other infiltrative airway diseases
redFlags: Significant central airway obstruction causing stridor or exertional breathlessness
Recurrent or severe lower respiratory infections from impaired clearance
Haemoptysis requiring exclusion of other airway pathology
Difficult airway during intubation or bronchoscopy due to rigid nodules
reference.prognosis: The condition is usually benign and slowly progressive; most patients have a good prognosis with symptomatic management, and significant airway compromise requiring intervention is uncommon.
pitfalls: Mistaking the nodular airway appearance for malignancy or amyloidosis without biopsy
Failing to recognise the diagnostic clue of posterior membrane sparing
Underestimating the risk of a difficult airway during instrumentation
Attributing chronic cough or recurrent infection to more common causes and overlooking the diagnosis
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Observation alone for the many asymptomatic patients, given the benign, slowly progressive course
Symptomatic relief of cough and wheeze with inhaled bronchodilators, humidification and cough suppression as needed
Prompt antibiotics and airway clearance for recurrent infections arising from impaired secretion clearance
Bronchoscopic debulking by laser, cryotherapy or mechanical removal of nodules for significant airway obstruction, anticipating hard tissue that makes instrumentation difficult
Periodic bronchoscopic and CT surveillance to monitor luminal narrowing and secretion retention
Exclude infiltrative mimics, particularly amyloidosis, given the overlapping submucosal nodular appearance
